newsitem.title: FRANCE: Chirac opens France's new Mitterrand library.
newsitem.headline: Chirac opens France's new Mitterrand library.

text.p: An uncharacteristically silent President Jacques Chirac on Tuesday inaugurated France's mammoth new Francois Mitterrand national library, named after his late book-loving predecessor who launched the costly project.

In low-key opening ceremonies, Chirac unveiled a plaque and toured the library complex accompanied by Mitterrand's widow Danielle and other dignitaries. But, in a jab at the Socialist Mitterrand, he made no speech.

The conservative Chirac, a devotee of Japanese art who shows little public interest in books, tried to block or delay construction of the complex during the early 1990s while he was mayor of Paris, library officials said.

Mitterrand, who left office in May 1995 and died last January, acknowledged near the end of his presidency that he had rushed construction so the complex would be too far along to be torn down when voters threw out France's Socialist government in 1993 general elections.

The costly steel and glass complex by the banks of the Seine, designed by architect Dominique Perrault, consists of four L-shaped glass towers, each 18 stories high, surrounding a sunken urban forest of wild pines, elms and birches. There are also six levels buried underground.

Officials said the project cost eight billion francs ($1.5 billion), well above initial projections, and will take another billion francs ($200 million) a year to operate, biting deeply into France's culture budget.

It is the last in a series of expensive and controversial Mitterrand public works projects which altered the landscape of the French capital, including the controversial glass pyramid entrance to the Louvre museum, sprawling science and music "cities" and the vast Bastille opera house.
The library has been the focus of controversy since Mitterrand first announced in July 1988 that France would build "a very large library of an entirely new type".
In a play on words on France's sleek TGV fast trains, it soon became known as the TGB or "Tres Grande Bibliotheque" -- the "very large library".

But the official opening has prompted a public outpouring of good feeling about the ungainly complex, focusing on its high-tech computers, elegant furnishings and sumptuous interior design, contrasting bold woodwork with huge steel-girded windows, concrete walls and deep orange-red carpeting.
Only one level of the building will initially be open to the general public, beginning on Friday. A second level will eventually be opened, but only to scholars.
The public spaces in the new library are nonetheless far larger than the existing national library's cramped quarters in the capital's second district.
The current library's main collection of 10 million volumes will be moved into the new complex at an average rate of 25,000 to 30,000 volumes a day over the next two years.

The old library will be renamed after Cardinal de Richelieu, who was chief minister to King Louis XIII from 1624 until his death in 1642. It will become France's main depository for maps, manuscripts, engravings, music, coins and theatrical items.
